X0.p: A category of humorous tales in which someone is embarrassed, thwarted, or made to look foolish.

X11.r: I must run through the village a couple of times more.” Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 224 No. 64.
X11.p: A man copies a friend's advice to feed red pepper to his slow donkey, and the donkey runs off; he then tries the pepper on himself, runs so fast he passes the donkey, and tells his wife to unload the donkey when it arrives.

X12.p: A man keeps being interrupted every time he tries to eat.

X12.1.p: A man who is repeatedly interrupted while eating answers others only in rhyming one-syllable words.

X21.r: (Cf. G60.) *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 257 No. 193; Italian Novella: Rotunda. Cf. Japanese: Ikeda.
X21.p: A man unknowingly eats human flesh: he consumes dried meat that turns out to be a dead man's body, which a Jew is carrying home for burial.

X31.r: *Wesselski Arlotto II 267 No. 216, Hodscha Nasreddin I 278 No. 314; Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 788f.; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
X31.p: A man dreams he finds treasure and marks the spot with his excrement; only the last part of the dream turns out to be true.

X31.1.r: Finds cat’s excrements. Italian Novella: Rotunda.
X31.1.p: A man dreams that he has become rich.

X31.2.p: A pig licks a sleeping man's lips, and the man thinks he is being kissed.

X32.p: Overdressed young men bet that a servant cannot carry a large bucket of water upstairs; they follow him and get soaked when he deliberately spills the dirty water.

X34.p: Someone uses an ointment that causes itching, as a prank or with comic results.

X52.p: A person is made ridiculous by being naked or exposed in public.

X52.1.p: A woman is publicly embarrassed when a monkey snatches off her wig.

X53.p: A man is given a humiliating ride on a hemp-dresser.

X100.r: Besides the motifs which follow, the entire series of motifs concerning fools (J1700—J2799) properly belongs here as well as where it is given.
X100.p: Humor that makes fun of physical disabilities or deformities.

X110.p: A category of humorous tales built on deafness, where misunderstandings between deaf people and others create the joke.

X111.p: A group of humorous tales about deaf men whose answers to others are absurd because they misunderstand what is said.

X111.1.r: B talks about his work and makes a gesture.—A follows the direction of the gesture and happens to find the animals. He returns and offers an injured animal to B in thanks. — B thinks that he is blamed for injuring the animals. Dispute. Taken to deaf judge. (Cf. X111.14.) *Type 1698A; Aarne FFC XX 16ff.; India: *Thompson-Balys.
X111.1.p: A man who is deaf asks about his lost animal, and the people he speaks with misunderstand him, creating a comic mix-up.

X111.2.r: Peasant’s wife arrives; thinks they say her food is too salty.—Daughter-in-law and father-in-law misunderstand each other. *Type 1698B; Aarne FFC XX 28ff.; India: *Thompson-Balys.
X111.2.p: Travelers ask a deaf peasant for directions, but he thinks they want to buy his oxen and answers accordingly.

X111.3.r: *Type 1698C; *Aarne FFC XX 29ff.; Wesselski Gonnella 118 No. 16; Nouvelles Récréations No. 10; Nouvelles de Sens No. 4.
X111.3.p: Two deaf men are each secretly told by a trickster that the other is hard of hearing, so when they meet they shout at each other until both think the other has lost his mind.

X111.4.r: Lord: Good morning, Peter.—Peasant: I come from Bingen.—L. What is the hog worth? —P. Two weeks from next Sunday (the wedding).—L. Shall I come to the wedding?—P. Three and a half gulden. *Type 1698D; *Aarne FFC XX 35ff.; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 719.
X111.4.p: A deaf peasant misunderstands a wedding invitation, so his answer or behavior is comically wrong for the occasion.

X111.5.r: Lord: Good day, Caspar. — Caspar: I am making a reel.—L. Good day, Caspar.—C. It is worth four pence. —L. Good day, Caspar.—C. Yes, my lord, whenever you wish. Type 1698E; *Aarne FFC XX 38ff.
X111.5.p: A deaf man on a bridge fails to hear what people say to him, leading to a comic misunderstanding.

X111.6.r: Finally—Nobleman: I wish you a thousand gallows and ropes around your neck.—Peasant: My lord, I wish you twice as many. Type 1698F; *Aarne FFC XX 39ff.
X111.6.p: A proud nobleman amuses himself by mocking a deaf man who cannot hear what is being said about him.

X111.7.r: Type 1698G; Aarne FFC XX 40, 76.—Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 189; India: Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 296.
X111.7.p: Words are misheard or not caught, and the mix-up leads to comic results; sometimes the people are only briefly inattentive, sometimes truly deaf.

X111.8.r: (The questions and answers often rhyme.) Type 1698H; Aarne FFC XX 41ff.
X111.8.p: A traveler asks a deaf man the way, but the man keeps talking about a bird he has caught in a tree and never answers the question.

X111.9.r: A. How are you?—B. I am dead. —Thank God! What have you eaten? — Poison, I think.—I hope it agrees with you. *Type 1698I; Aarne FFC XX 50ff.; India: Thompson-Balys.
X111.9.p: A deaf man plans a visit to the sick with set questions and answers in mind, but the sick person replies in ways he did not expect.

X111.10.r: “A woodchopper.” The workman answers the traveler’s courtesies with remarks about his work. (Cf. X111.8.) Type 1698J; Aarne FFC XX 51ff., cf. 67ff., 72, 75 (Types 12, 13, 16, 18).
X111.10.p: A deaf man takes a greeting of "Good day" as something else, and his reply is comically off.

X111.11.p: A joke in which a buyer and a deaf seller misunderstand each other and their answers do not match.

X111.12.p: A deaf young man, who is to become a parson, answers the questions in an unintelligible way, yet is praised anyway.

X111.13.r: The drunken priest says, “In the morning I take a drink of rum and afterwards four or five little drinks.” Type 1698M.
X111.13.p: A deaf bishop is the central figure of a comic tale built on his deafness and the misunderstandings it causes.

X111.14.r: (Cf. X111.1.) *Chauvin VII 113 No. 381; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
X111.14.p: Deaf litigants and a deaf judge at a lawsuit misunderstand one another, so the trial becomes comic confusion.

X111.15.r: One asks name of town; another replies, “This is Wesley.” Another says, “I thought it was Thursday.” Third says, “So am I; let’s have a drink.” U.S.: Baughman.
X111.15.p: Travelers pass through a place called Wesley, and the humor depends on a misunderstanding about it or its people.

X112.p: A deaf husband tells his deaf wife to prepare a certain dish, and each misunderstands the other, so the wrong food results.

X113.p: A household of deaf people constantly misunderstands one another, causing repeated misunderstandings and quarrels.

X120.p: A general heading for jokes whose humor comes from poor eyesight, such as people who see wrongly or cannot see at all.

X121.r: Husband: “See everything double except your husband.” Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 186 No. 358.
X121.p: A wife with poor eyesight sees two of everything, such as two plates where there is one, and imagines two men are with her.

X121.1.r: really the only one. Chauvin II 196 No. 22.
X121.1.p: A squint-eyed son is sent by his father to fetch the only bottle of rare wine. Seeing two bottles, he breaks one so that his father will not be shown to have lied about there being two.

X122.r: “He saw only half a horse; otherwise he would have valued it at a mark.” Bédier Fabliaux 123; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
X122.p: A one-eyed man is hired to appraise a horse and values it at only half a mark, a foolish judgment made because of his poor sight.

X123.p: A blind man asks a bull whether he is on the right road, and the bull butts him and knocks him down. The man complains that it was unnecessary, since a simple yes or no would have answered him.

X123.1.p: A blind man gets home in a ridiculous way, such as hanging on an ox's tail, after being misled by the animal or by his own blindness.

X124.p: A nearsighted knight attacks his own servant, thinking him to be an enemy, and runs his lance into the servant's backside.

X124.1.p: A blind man hits a woman, mistaking her for a buffalo.

X124.2.p: A blind son-in-law visits his wife's family and runs into trouble because he cannot see.

X125.p: Blind men who are trying to kill pigs with clubs end up hitting each other instead.

X128.p: A blind man who finds himself in an awkward position pretends that he can see.

X130.p: Jokes about other physical disabilities not covered by the preceding categories.

X131.r: U.S.: *Baughman; Danish: MS in Danske Folkemindesamling (Grundtvig No. 166).
X131.p: A family in which each member has his mouth twisted to a different side; their attempts to blow out a light fail because of this.

X133.p: A man calls a gathering of everyone with a long nose.

X135.p: Humor based on stuttering, in which a person's speech difficulty is the source of the joke.

X135.1.p: Four stutterers each believe the other three are laughing at him.

X135.2.p: A stutterer tries to raise an alarm but cannot get the words out.

X137.p: Humor based on a person's ugliness.

X141.p: A blind man, a lame man, and a deaf man are proposed or used as witnesses in court, and the joke lies in their unfitness to testify.

X142.p: Humor based on a person being very short.

X142.1.p: A dwarf king falls into a porridge pot at the court of a human king.

X142.2.p: A dwarf poet is forced to swim in the drinking-horn of a human being.

X142.3.p: A very small ambassador is put on a horse with long stirrups and is too busy keeping his seat to speak.

X142.4.p: A short magistrate wears a tall helmet, which makes him look absurd.

X143.p: Humor based on a person being lame.

X143.1.p: A lame man is taken on a hunt in a wheelchair and still beats the dogs home when they tree a ghost or when a bear chases them.

X145.p: A joke about someone whose singing is so bad that it is funny to listen to.

X145.1.p: A self-centred singer with a dismal, unpleasant voice is paid to have one listener who sits and hears him sing.

X151.p: A joke about people who are very fat, using their size as the source of humor.

X151.1.p: Six short, fat husbands and six tall, fat wives are married, and on the wedding day the husbands absurdly try to kiss their wives over the threshold.

X151.2.p: A man is so large and clumsy that he can only fish from his window, because he cannot get out into the street to do it.

X200.p: A general category of jokes that make fun of craftsmen and sellers in their trades.

X210.p: A general category of jokes that make fun of millers.

X211.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 785; Fb “møller” II 649; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
X211.p: Jokes portray millers as thieves who cheat their customers by stealing some of their grain or flour.

X212.p: A miller is honest and so ends up poor, and a baker wonders how a former miller could be a beggar, reasoning that farmers should be beggars instead.

X212.1.p: A priest praises the poor miller for his honesty, saying that if he had been like the rest of the congregation he would have become rich.

X213.p: A joke explaining why there are no millers in hell: a mad dog is put in hell in place of a miller, who is in a sack.

X214.p: Monks take revenge on millers: drunken millers are made to dance by the monks, and millers are lured into a monastery and beaten.

X220.p: A general category of jokes that make fun of tailors.

X221.p: A tailor steals cloth but is careless about where he hides it: he sews the stolen piece onto the outside of his coat, thinking it is on the inside.

X221.1.p: A thieving tailor cuts a piece from his own coat, mistaking it for the stolen cloth.

X221.2.p: A thieving tailor manages to hide stolen cloth even inside his needle-and-thread tube.

X222.r: **B. Salditt Hessische Blätter f. Vksk. XXX—XXXI 88.
X222.p: A joke that always links the tailor with a goat.

X223.p: Tailors are cowardly soldiers who, when war comes, run home to their needles instead of fighting.

X230.p: A general category of jokes that make fun of butchers.

X231.p: A butcher is puzzled that a customer who has bought his meat for seven years is still alive, implying the meat was bad or the joke is on the butcher's cooking.

X240.p: General jokes that mock shoemakers and cobblers as a trade.

X241.p: A cobbler who is ugly is the target of the joke; he keeps threatening to hurl his last, the wooden foot-shaped form used for shoemaking, at people.

X242.r: Wienert FFC LVI 39; Halm Aesop No. 136.
X242.p: A shoemaker drinks far more than his share of a lying drink that was mixed for everyone to share equally, so the joke is on his greed.

X250.p: General jokes that mock artisans and tradesmen other than cobblers, such as weavers, barbers, and fishermen.

X251.1.p: Explains why there are no weavers in hell: the devils were so annoyed by the weavers' noisy looms that they refused to admit them.

X252.1.p: A customer runs away when the barber tries to treat his cuts with cobwebs.

X252.2.p: A barber stops bleeding from cuts by using the hair he has cut off.

X253.1.p: Anecdotes about how talkative and abusive the fishwives of Paris were when they scolded others.

X300.p: General heading for jokes that mock people by their professions rather than by their social class as such.

X311.p: A woman sees a crowd of law students and reasons that if there are so many lawyers, great harm will follow, since the one lawyer in her village has already ruined almost everyone.

X312.r: Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 95 No. 819*; cf. U.S.: Baughman.
X312.p: A beggar scares a stingy lawyer into giving him money by describing all the lawyers who are in hell.

X313.r: U.S.: Baughman; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 134 No. 1583*.
X313.p: A dying man arranges for a lawyer and a notary to stand on either side of his deathbed, a joke that makes them seem like the two thieves beside Christ on the cross.

X314.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 127; Crane Vitry 155 No. 52; Scala Celi 7b No. 47; Alphabet No. 483.
X314.p: A lawyer who tries to do legal business without lying fails; in the tale he joins a religious order and then tries to carry on his work honestly.

X315.r: Crane Vitry 149f. No. 39; Scala Celi 7b No. 48; Herbert III 77 No. 200, 462 No. 94, 497 No. 238, 499 No. 262; Alphabet No. 41; Mensa Philosophica No. 147.
X315.p: A dying lawyer, on his deathbed, still tries to delay the end by saying he appeals.

X315.1.r: Crane Vitry 150 No. 40; Scala Celi 7b No. 45; Mensa Philosophica No. 148.
X315.1.p: A dying lawyer asks for a delay, as if he could postpone death the way he postpones lawsuits.

X316.r: Crane Vitry 148 No. 36; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
X316.p: Nero has reserved a place in hell for lawyers.

X317.p: A lawyer who has fallen into the mud is left there, because once the rescuers learn he is a lawyer they decide he is not worth saving. The joke mocks lawyers as unwelcome.

X318.p: A lawyer who has died is found to have no tongue, because he sold it while alive. The joke says lawyers sell their words for money.

X319.p: A general heading for assorted jokes that poke fun at lawyers.

X319.1.p: A skilled lawyer argues so persuasively for a client who is plainly guilty that the client starts to doubt his own guilt.

X330.p: A general heading for jokes that poke fun at magistrates, meaning judges or local officials of law.

X331.p: A magistrate confesses to a priest that he is guilty of every sin connected with the senses. When the priest says there are only five senses, the magistrate replies that he needs two more than other people.

X332.p: A foreigner is amazed that a city has so many judges and yet has not been destroyed. The joke implies judges are harmful to a place.

X350.p: A general heading for jokes that poke fun at teachers.

X351.p: A music teacher charges twice as much to students who have already studied music. The joke is that the second fee pays him to make them forget what they learned before.

X370.p: A general heading for jokes that poke fun at scholars and learned people.

X371.p: A man who has mastered all seven liberal arts ends up begging from a wagoner. He is poor because his learning does not earn money, and only his one practical skill supports his family.

X372.p: A general heading for jokes that poke fun at doctors.

X372.1.p: A doctor treats a racing heartbeat so badly that the patient stops breathing altogether.

X372.2.p: A doctor cures a snakebite by cutting off the patient's head.

X372.3.p: A doctor prescribes eyedrops for a stomachache so the patient can see what he is eating.

X372.4.p: A foolish doctor performs an operation that accomplishes nothing.

X372.4.1.p: A man whose cheeks are stuffed with food is operated on to remove the swellings, which were only the food in his mouth.

X372.5.p: A doctor summoned to a sick man at once orders the funeral arrangements, showing he expects the man to die.

X410.r: *Types 1725—1824; **Kristensen Vore Fædres Kirketjeneste (Aarhus, 1899); *Fb “præst” II 884a; West Indies: Flowers 583.
X410.p: A general heading for jokes that poke fun at parsons, meaning Protestant or country clergymen.

X411.p: A parson is so bad at preaching that the congregation flees in the middle of his sermon.

X411.1.p: A sexton's dog steals a sausage from the parson's pocket during his sermon, so the parson runs away in fright.

X411.2.p: The sexton slips a needle into the communion bread, and the parson jerks his hand back in pain and flees.

X411.3.p: The sexton arranges a wasp nest so the parson sits down on it, and the angry wasps chase him away.

X412.p: A tame bear is tied to the church bells, so when the bells are rung the bear is pulled about and the church is disrupted.

X413.p: A parson who is one-eyed and works in a dim church mixes up the couples and marries the old man to the girl and the old woman to the boy.

X414.p: A parson rides an ox into church to imitate Christ entering Jerusalem, and the sexton jabs the ox with a needle, making it bolt.

X415.p: A hog is accidentally locked in the church all week; when the congregation arrives, the hog runs between the parson's legs and carries him out.

X416.r: Those that see this laugh. He wins the wager. *Type 1828*; Wesselski Morlini 297 No. 44.
X416.p: A parson preaches so movingly that half the congregation weeps and half laughs, because his clothes have been torn at the back without his knowing.

X417.r: The parson preaches, “What is the life of man?” and therewith brings his hand down on the altar-bread: “Pure butter!” Type 1836*.
X417.p: A parson smears butter on his hand, because rascals have spread butter on the communion bread.

X418.p: A parson is supposed to let a dove fly in church, but the dove dies in his pocket.

X421.p: During the blessing of a grave the parson's ox breaks loose, and someone says, "Now the devil has him."

X422.r: The parson: “On the last day he will arise.” One of the coffin-makers: “Did I say that?” Type 1699*.
X422.p: A corpse arrives with its feet cut off, because the coffin-maker had to fit him to a coffin that was too short.

X424.r: With the gouty parson on his back he comes upon the thieves who, thinking it is their companion with the sheep, call out, “Is he fat?” The sexton: “Fat or lean, here he is!” *Type 1791; *BP III 395; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 82; Scala Celi 101b No. 547; Alphabet No. 333; U.S., England: *Baughman; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1791, Legends No. 889.
X424.p: A sexton hears thieves in the cemetery cracking nuts and mistakes the sound for the devil cracking bones.

X424.1.p: Robbers mistake a man for the devil; when the supposed sheep speaks and says "Gently, gently!", they run off in terror.

X425.p: A parson who insists there is no devil is shown otherwise when a bear-showman lets the bear climb into the pulpit and the parson takes it for the devil.

X426.p: An innkeeper says that if his son were only a fool he would let him study to become a priest, mocking the priesthood.

X427.p: A priest complains of a bad year because there are few funerals; everyone else is glad of the community's good health, but he mourns his lost burial fees.

X428.p: Monks and priests quarrel over chickens and eggs: monks eat eggs and make chickens expensive, while priests eat hens and make eggs dear.

X431.r: Overnight at the peasant’s house. The hungry parson hunts the porridge in the dark, guided by a rope the sexton has given him. Series of accidents. *Type 1775; Fb “seng” III 187a.
X431.p: A hungry parson sneaks to a porridge-pot and gets into trouble over the food meant for others.

X431.1.p: A foolish man, while visiting, tries to take honey from a jug at night.

X434.p: A joke in which a parson is embarrassed or made to look foolish, leaving him speechless or red-faced.

X434.1.p: A parson claims Jesus's loaves were as big as mountains, and a mason jokingly asks what oven could bake loaves that large.

X434.2.r: The parson asks the boy: “What does your father say when you begin to eat?” Boy: “You young devil, etc.” *Type 1841.
X434.2.p: A joke about a parson's grace before a meal, where the saying of grace turns out to be the punchline that embarrasses him.

X435.p: A parson preaches a sermon and a boy takes his words and applies them in a cheeky, literal or present-day way, making the parson look foolish.

X435.1.r: Variants: (a) What evil did Adam do?—He (shoemaker) made my shoes too small. (b) What kind of man was Moses? He was a day laborer. *Type 1833A; *Wesselski Arlotto II 233 No. 113.
X435.1.p: A parson asks what David says, and the boy answers that David says to pay your old debts.

X435.2.p: A parson asks where the father stayed, and the boy answers that he stayed behind to hold the oxen.

X435.3.p: A parson asks where Christ was when he was neither in heaven nor on earth, and the boy answers that he was in the willow grove looking for a stick to beat people who ask foolish questions.

X435.4.r: The priest’s example: the three cows. The boy: “The Holy Ghost has just had a calf.” Type 1833D; England: Baughman.
X435.4.p: A boy is asked to name the persons of the Trinity, and his answer provides a comic or cheeky list in place of the correct one.

X435.5.r: When the parson preaches about the rich man who went to hell, the boy calls out, “Then he took my coat along!” *Type 1832.
X435.5.p: A boy riding with a rich man goes into church and leaves his coat lying on the sled, applying a sermon about the rich man to the situation.

X436.r: *Type 1834; Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 243 No. 539; *Crane Vitry 157 No. 56; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 576; Fb “prædiken” II 882; Scala Celi 25a No. 164;—Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys.
X436.p: A parson thinks an old woman is weeping because his singing has moved her, but she is actually sad about a lost goat that his singing reminded her of.

X438.p: A smith tells the parson he has dreamed that St. Peter would not let him into heaven until he had seen a parson, and that there were no parsons in heaven because they were all in hell.

X438.1.p: A devout woman and a priest tell each other their dreams, and the priest dreams that all devout women are in hell.

X441.p: A parson, during the mass, gives instructions aloud to the sexton, who is meant to be cooking, so the instructions become part of the service.

X441.1.r: Rector confesses his sacristan: “Have you drunk the wine designated for the mass?” — “I can’t hear you.” Exchange of places. Sacristan asks rector: “Have you kissed my wife?” — “Really, I can’t hear you.” Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2451*; Rumanian: Schullerus FFC LXXVIII No. 1777*.
X441.1.p: During the mass, the sexton keeps replying that he cannot hear the priest's instructions.

X442.p: The church bell breaks, and during mass the priest's patron whistles in place of ringing the bell.

X443.p: A joke about a parson who is a poor horseman and is thrown or troubled while riding.

X443.1.p: A chaplain tries to ride a mule that bucks him off.

X445.p: A parson pauses during his sermon to refresh himself with a drink or other indulgence.

X445.1.p: A parson takes a drink of liquor in the middle of his sermon.

X445.2.p: A parson takes a chew of tobacco in the middle of his sermon.

X451.p: A rooster crows in the church, which wakes the sexton (the church caretaker), who then starts singing. The joke mocks the church staff as lazy or sleepy.

X452.p: A joke where a parson is excused from preaching because the congregation already knows what he would say. The point is that people who already understand need no teaching.

X452.1.r: He has performed no new miracles.” *Wesselski Arlotto I 188 No. 8; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
X452.1.p: A parson tells his congregation there is no need to preach about a saint again, since he already described the saint's life and works the previous year.

X453.r: Refuses to say, “I’m not worthy” at communion. Italian Novella: Rotunda.
X453.p: A joke built on a woman named "Worthy" whose name is used as a pun or punchline. The humor depends on the wordplay of her name.

X454.p: A chapel is given fifty blows as its endowment for the friar. The joke mocks friars by turning a gift into a beating.

X457.p: A general heading for jokes that make fun of monks.

X457.1.p: A bishop is willing to admit a castrated man as a monk, and he wishes that all men were in the same condition. The joke is a bawdy jab at monks and clergy.

X459.p: A general heading for miscellaneous jokes that make fun of parsons and clergy.

X459.1.p: A man takes what he believes is a divine call to become a minister, though it may be a mistake or misreading of signs.

X459.1.1.p: A young man plowing a cornfield sees the letters "P. C." formed by clouds and takes them as a sign to become a minister. He asks to be ordained, but the minister explains the letters mean "plow corn" rather than "preach Christ."

X460.p: A general heading for jokes about members of professions other than the clergy.

X461.p: A general heading for jokes that make fun of fortune-tellers.

X461.1.r: (Cf. J1062.) Herbert III 22 No. 186; Crane Vitry 250 No. 266.
X461.1.p: A fortune-teller tells others how to get rich but never becomes wealthy himself. The joke mocks the gap between his advice and his own life.

X500.p: A general heading for jokes that make fun of social groups other than the professions already listed.

X510.p: A general heading for jokes that make fun of usurers, that is, moneylenders who charge high interest.

X511.p: Custom holds that a dead person may not be buried until someone says something good about him. Only a barber is willing to praise a dead usurer, saying he had a good beard.

X512.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) Nos. 193, 194; Crane Vitry 207 No. 179; Scala Celi 168b No. 959; Alphabet No. 792.
X512.p: A parson asks members of each trade to stand for a special blessing, but when he calls for usurers, none of them answer.

X513.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 191; cf. Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 213.
X513.p: A youth paid by a usurer protests the priest's claim that the devil would carry all usurers off to hell. He declares instead that the devil will not carry them but will drag them by the legs.

X514.r: (Cf. X521.) Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 190; Irish: Beal XXI 326, cf. O’Suilleabhain 74.
X514.p: A usurer's corpse will allow only other usurers to carry it, refusing to be moved by anyone else. The joke mocks usurers' greed even in death.

X516.p: A usurer supports sermons against usury, hoping they will drive his competitors out of business. The joke exposes his hypocrisy.

X520.p: Jokes that make fun of prostitutes.

X521.p: A joke in which only a prostitute is considered fit to carry the body of a dead prostitute, so the other people refuse the task.

X530.p: Jokes that make fun of beggars.

X531.p: A joke in which beggars who fake being crippled rush away from a holy shrine so they will not be cured and lose the income their disability brings.

X540.p: Jokes that make fun of madmen or the mentally ill.

X541.p: A joke in which lunatics are deliberately made to live together as a prank or amusement.

X550.p: Jokes that make fun of members of secret societies.

X551.p: Jokes that make fun of freemasons.

X583.p: Jokes that make fun of travelers.

X584.p: Jokes that make fun of hunters.

X584.1.p: A hunter who is chased by a bear back to camp claims he brought the bear in alive, explaining that he did not want to carry it.

X600.p: Jokes that make fun of whole races or nations.

X610.p: Jokes that make fun of Jews.

X611.r: Someone cries, “Clothes are being auctioned off in hell.” *Type 2403; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1868*; cf. U.S.: Baughman (X597.1, X902).
X611.p: A joke explaining how the Jews were supposedly driven out of heaven.

X613.p: A trickster interrupts a Jewish wedding ceremony and then seduces the bride.

X650.p: Jokes that make fun of other races or nations not covered elsewhere.

X651.r: Hungarians win. Wesselski Bebel II 149 No. 160.
X651.p: A joke in which the lice of Strassburg and the lice of Hungary fight a battle against each other.

X652.p: A joke in which a caretaker of an estate, recently sold to a Bavarian, sits among the pigs in order to learn the Bavarian language.

X661.r: Wienert FFC LVI 39; Halm Aesop No. 141.
X661.p: A tale explaining why Arabians are said to be liars: the god Hermes and his wagon of lies break down in Arabia, so the lies spread there.

X680.p: Jokes that make fun of various cities and their inhabitants.

X681.r: P. Sébillot and H. Gaidoz Le Blason Populaire de la France.
X681.p: One city uses spiteful nicknames or insulting names for another city, and the jokes about those cities rely on them.

X700.p: A general category of humorous stories and jokes about sex and sexual matters.

X750.r: *Types 1475—1499; Hdwb. d. Abergl. I 334 s.v. “Alte Jungfer”.
X750.p: A group of jokes that make fun of unmarried women who are past the usual age of marriage.

X751.p: A church order forbids young men of the parish to marry girls from other parishes, a joke about the lack of suitors for old maids.

X752.p: An old maid sleeps between a bundle of straw standing in for her husband and a dog standing in for her child; she pushes the straw away and falls out of bed herself.

X753.p: A young man promises to marry an old maid if she sits all night on the roof, and she falls down.

X754.p: An old maid eats a meal of beans, and one of her three remaining teeth breaks off.

X755.p: A wolf carries off the old maid, but she keeps him as her husband.

X756.p: A mother tries to train her old maid daughter to speak correctly and politely.

X760.p: A group of jokes about the ways young people court and try to win one another.

X800.p: A general category of humorous stories in which drunkenness is the source of the joke.

X811.p: A drunk man wakes lying under his bed and believes he is laid out in his shroud; the scare cures him of drinking.

X812.p: A drunk man goes to the king and offers to buy an island.

X813.p: A drunk man goes to a wedding, falls asleep before reaching it, and at home praises the wedding as if he had attended.

X814.p: Drunk men each try to see the other safely home, and neither manages it.

X815.p: A drunk man sees everything spinning and waits for his house to come to him instead of walking home.

X816.p: A drunk woman thinks she has gone to heaven because she hears someone playing a lyre.

X818.p: Drunk recruits attack a haystack as if it were an enemy in war.

X821.p: Drunken volunteer firemen make a mess of putting out a fire.

X900.p: A general category of humorous stories built on obvious lies and wild exaggeration.

X901.r: Amusing results. Chauvin V 278 No. 161; *BP II 371, 509; Köhler-Bolte I 322; India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Vai): Ellis 239 No. 46.
X901.p: A man who tells only one lie a year is believed, because people trust him for being generally truthful.

X902.p: A habitual liar repeats a lie so often that he ends up believing it himself.

X903.p: A lie is told as a catch tale: a story built to trap a listener into expecting a nonsensical or endless ending.

X904.p: A storyteller shrinks his tale to a smaller, more modest lie after being questioned or doubted.

X904.1.p: A liar cuts his lie down in size when his brother steps on his toes, a signal reminding him of his habit of lying.

X904.2.p: A liar makes his yarn smaller when someone challenges him to prove it.

X905.r: Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
X905.p: Contests in which people compete to tell the biggest or most outrageous lies.

X905.1.r: Type 1920C; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1920D*; Russian: Andrejev No. 1920D*; Prussian: Plenzat 78; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 119 No. 27; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 51 No. 89; India: *Thompson-Balys.
X905.1.p: In a lying contest, a master is tricked into saying "You lie!", which means he has lost the contest.

X905.2.p: The greatest liar is rewarded by being made king of Schlaraffenland, the legendary land of plenty.

X905.3.p: A person gains ownership of property because of an unusually clever lie he tells.

X905.4.r: Type 1920B; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 308ff. No. 18, FFC CXXVIII 260ff. No. 160.
X905.4.p: A man says he has no time to lie today, and then lies anyway.

X905.4.1.p: A boy plans to deceive his uncle by first getting him to climb a tree; the act of climbing up is itself the deception.

X906.r: Liar tells of shooting large number of animals with one shot (an odd number, usually 99). When asked why he did not make it a round number (or an even hundred), he replies indignantly that he would not lie for one pigeon (rabbit). U.S.: *Baughman.
X906.p: A person refuses to tell even a small lie, not even for a trifling reason.

X907.r: Rewards him poorly. Servant exposes him. Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
X907.p: A man has his servant back up his lies by confirming them.

X907.1.p: A second liar confirms and supports the lie told by the first liar.

X908.r: (Often with answer: “Many fried fish.”) (First ed. X925.) Type 1920A; *BP II 371; Fb “vesterhav” III 1042b, “a” III 1187b; Indonesian: DeVries Volksverhalen II 377.
X908.p: A lie in which someone claims the sea has burned up or dried away.

X909.p: Other tales about liars that do not fit the categories above.

X909.1.p: A liar who cannot be cured of lying, no matter how he is confronted.

X909.1.1.p: A church member, rebuked for lying, tells another lie while claiming to be sorry for his weakness, saying he has wept barrels of tears over it.

X909.2.p: A liar outdoes tricksters who try to catch him by continuing the very lie they invented to trap him.

X910.r: (Cf. F500—F599.) For bibliography of American hero material see Harold Felton Legends of Paul Bunyan (New York, 1947).
X910.p: A tall tale about an extraordinarily remarkable man, told as a joke or exaggeration rather than as true history.

X911.p: A joking lie about how a remarkable hero was born, with outlandish circumstances presented as fact.

X912.p: A joking lie about the hero's infancy and boyhood, showing him doing astonishing things as a child.

X913.p: A joking lie about the death of an extraordinary man, told with absurd exaggeration.

X916.p: A joking lie describing a remarkable person who has unusually large or unusual body parts.

X920.p: A general heading for tall tales in which a man is said to be exceptionally large or strong.

X921.p: A joking lie about a person who is absurdly tall.

X922.p: A joking lie about a large person who weighs an absurdly great amount.

X923.p: A joking lie about a large person with an absurdly great girth or waist size.

X924.p: A joking lie about a person who is absurdly thin.

X930.p: A general heading for tall tales about a remarkable person's bodily powers and everyday habits, exaggerated for humor.

X931.p: A joking lie about a person who eats an absurdly large amount.

X932.p: A joking lie about a person who can drink an absurdly large amount.

X933.p: A joking lie about a person who chews with absurd power or quantity.

X934.p: A joking lie about a person who spits with remarkable distance or amount.

X935.p: A joking lie about a person who can blow with absurd force or volume.

X936.p: A joking lie about a person whose hearing is absurdly keen.

X937.p: A joking lie about a person whose voice is absurdly loud or powerful.

X938.p: A joking lie about a person whose eyesight is absurdly keen.

X939.p: A catch-all heading for other joking lies about a person's unusual senses or bodily powers.

X940.p: A tall tale in which a man is boasted of as remarkably strong, the exaggeration serving as the joke.

X941.p: A lie about a man who is a remarkable lifter, so strong that he can lift impossible weights.

X941.1.p: A lie in which a strong man lifts an entire village.

X941.2.p: A lie in which a strong man fights someone on the palm of an old woman's hand.

X941.3.p: A lie in which a man puts an elephant, or a camel, in his pocket as a curiosity to show his friends.

X941.4.p: A lie in which a wind blows a group of people into a woman's eye.

X942.p: A lie about a man who is a remarkable carrier, able to carry impossibly heavy loads.

X942.1.p: A lie in which a man ties up 700 camels in one corner of his sheet and carries them.

X943.p: A lie about a man who is a remarkable thrower, able to hurl things impossibly far or with impossible force.

X943.1.p: A lie in which a beautiful girl sits on a huge lotus flower, holding a big elephant in each hand, eating them and throwing them off in turn.

X943.1.1.p: A lie in which a child throws out the carcass of an elephant.

X944.p: A lie about a man who is a remarkable catcher, able to catch impossibly large or fast things.

X945.p: A lie about a man who is a remarkable hitter or striker, whose blows are impossibly powerful.

X946.p: A lie about a man who is a remarkable breaker, able to smash or break impossibly strong things.

X947.p: A lie about a man who is a remarkable bender, able to bend impossibly hard things.

X948.p: A lie about a man who is a remarkable twister, able to twist impossibly hard things.

X951.p: A lie about a man who is a remarkable squeezer, whose grip is impossibly powerful.

X952.p: A lie about a man who is a remarkable pincher; the hero marks logs by pinching a piece out of the end of each one.

X953.p: A lie about a man who is a strong puller, able to pull impossibly heavy loads.

X953.1.p: A lie in which a man draws sixty (or three hundred) carts of wood at once.

X954.p: A tall tale about a remarkably strong man who is a pusher, able to push or shove things with enormous force.

X955.p: A tall tale about a remarkably strong man who is a killer, with exaggerated feats of killing through sheer strength.

X958.p: A tall tale in which a strong hero is credited with creating lakes, rivers, valleys or other landforms through his actions.

X959.p: A tall tale about other extraordinary physical reactions of a strong man, exaggerated beyond what is possible.

X959.1.r: (Cf. D1562.3, F610.) Korean: Zong in-Sob 67 No. 37.
X959.1.p: A tall tale in which a hero's strength is so great that when he breaks wind, the force knocks down a wall.

X960.p: A general tall tale heading for exaggerated claims about a remarkable person's skills and abilities.

X961.p: A tall tale about a person with extraordinary bodily skills, far beyond what any real person could do.

X964.p: A tall tale about a person who is an impossibly remarkable swimmer.

X965.p: A tall tale about a person who is an impossibly remarkable diver.

X966.p: A tall tale about a person who is an impossibly remarkable jumper.

X967.p: A tall tale about a person who is an impossibly remarkable kicker, able to kick with unbelievable force or distance.

X971.p: A tall tale about a person who is an impossibly remarkable oarsman, rowing with unbelievable speed or strength.

X972.p: A tall tale about a person who is an impossibly remarkable fighter.

X973.p: A tall tale about a person who is an impossibly remarkable wrestler.

X980.p: A general tall tale heading for exaggerated claims about a person's skill at an occupation or profession.

X982.p: A tall tale about a blacksmith of impossible skill, whose work is exaggerated beyond belief.

X983.p: A tall tale about a man of impossible skill at skinning, who flays buffalo alive and turns them loose so they grow new skins.

X986.p: A tall tale about an axeman of impossible skill, whose chopping is exaggerated beyond belief.

X986.1.p: A tall tale in which an axe made of wax is used to cut down a jungle.

X987.p: A tall tale about a logger of impossible skill, whose logging feats are exaggerated beyond belief.

X991.p: A tall tale about a remarkably skilled rock driller who wins a contest against a steam drill but dies in the effort.

X994.p: A tall tale about a carpenter with impossible, exaggerated skill.

X1001.p: A tall tale about a thresher (a farm worker who threshes grain) with impossible, exaggerated skill.

X1002.p: A tall tale about a man who handles a whip with impossible, exaggerated skill.

X1003.p: A tall tale about a roper (a cowboy who throws a lasso) with impossible, exaggerated skill.

X1004.p: A tall tale about a rider with impossible, exaggerated riding skill.

X1004.1.p: A tall tale in which a man rides an unusual or unlikely animal, such as a lion or a deer.

X1004.2.p: A tall tale in which a man rides a cyclone (a violent windstorm).

X1005.p: A tall tale about a cook with impossible, exaggerated cooking skill.

X1010.p: A tall tale about a person with exaggerated, impossibly sharp mental abilities.

X1011.p: A tall tale about a person who is an extraordinary inventor.

X1012.p: A tall tale about a person who shows impossibly clever ingenuity or resourcefulness in getting out of trouble or doing work.

X1012.1.p: A tall tale in which axes grind themselves into shape on boulders rolling down a hill.

X1020.p: A tall tale about the impossibly extraordinary belongings of a remarkable man.

X1021.p: A tall tale about the extraordinary clothing a remarkable man wears.

X1021.1.p: A tall tale about rubber boots, or similar footwear, that bounce with impossible springiness.

X1022.p: A tall tale about other impossibly extraordinary personal belongings of a remarkable person.

X1023.p: A tall tale about extraordinary equipment owned by a remarkable man.

X1024.p: A tall tale about impossibly extraordinary tools owned by a remarkable man.

X1025.p: A tall tale about impossibly extraordinary machinery owned by a remarkable man.

X1030.p: A tall tale in which the boastful man owns buildings of huge, impossible size.

X1030.1.p: A tall tale in which the boastful man's building is described as unusually great, far beyond any normal size.

X1031.r: (First ed. X1033.1.) Chauvin VII 57 No. 77; U.S.: *Baughman, *Folk-Say I 62.
X1031.p: A tall tale in which the boastful man has a kitchen of impossible size.

X1031.1.p: A tall tale in which the great kitchen is fitted with equipment of impossible size.

X1031.1.1.p: A tall tale in which the great kitchen contains an enormous kettle.

X1031.2.p: A tall tale in which the great kitchen needs an impossibly large staff to run it.

X1031.3.p: A tall tale in which enormous amounts of cooking are done in the great kitchen.

X1031.4.p: A tall tale in which enormous amounts of baking are done in the great kitchen.

X1031.4.1.p: A tall tale in which a man skates across a griddle, greasing it by pulling a strip of bacon under his feet in the great kitchen.

X1031.5.p: A tall tale in which the great kitchen turns out other extraordinary foods of impossible size or quantity.

X1031.6.p: A tall tale about the food tastes of the workers, such as loggers who eat the same unusual dish at every meal.

X1031.7.p: A tall tale in which the great kitchen produces enormous piles of garbage.

X1032.p: A tall tale in which the great dining quarters are of impossible size, as told of Paul Bunyan.

X1033.p: A tall tale in which the great bunkhouse, where workers sleep, is of impossible size.

X1035.p: A tall tale in which the great hotel is of impossible size.

X1036.p: A tall tale in which the great stable is of impossible size.

X1036.1.p: A tall tale in which a cow's calf grows up and has its own calf before it can walk the short distance to its stall in the great stable.

X1060.p: A tall tale in which the boastful man owns other possessions of impossible size or quality.

X1061.p: A tall tale in which the boastful man owns a boat or ship of impossible size.

X1061.1.r: (First ed. X1031.) Type 1960H; BP II 516; U.S.: *Baughman.
X1061.1.p: A tall tale in which the great ship is described as impossibly large.

X1070.p: A tall tale in which a remarkably extraordinary man's family or household is described in exaggerated terms.

X1071.p: A tall tale about a giant's wedding in which the giant has sixty daughters to marry off.

X1080.p: A tall tale in which a remarkable man is said to have had astonishing jobs or occupations.

X1081.p: A tall tale about a remarkably huge or astonishing logging operation, such as an impossibly large timber harvest.

X1082.p: A tall tale in which a man is said to be an amazing manufacturer of goods, with exaggerated production.

X1082.1.p: A tall tale about a remarkable sawmill operator who produces an impossibly large amount of lumber.

X1082.2.p: A tall tale about a remarkable dairyman whose milk or dairy production is absurdly exaggerated.

X1083.p: A tall tale about a remarkable steel worker whose feats in steel work are absurdly exaggerated.

X1084.p: A tall tale about a remarkable oil drilling operator whose drilling feats are absurdly exaggerated.

X1100.p: A tall tale about a remarkably skilled hunter or fisherman whose exploits are absurdly exaggerated.

X1110.r: (First ed. X921.) *Types 1890—1909; Wesselski Märchen 226f.; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 312.
X1110.p: A tall tale about a wonderfully successful hunt in which the hunter bags impossible quantities or strange catches.

X1110.1.r: (First ed. X921.0.1.) Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 313.
X1110.1.p: A joking reversal of the wonderful hunt in which the hunter has an unlucky hunt and catches nothing or meets misfortune.

X1111.p: A tall tale in which a hunter shoots so many ducks at once that they fill a ramrod-length row, that is, his gun's ramrod is filled with ducks.

X1112.p: A tall tale in which a hunter wading in water catches fish that end up inside his boots.

X1114.p: A tall tale in which a man lays a bag by a hole in a fence and all the hares run into it.

X1114.1.p: A tall tale in which two hares running into each other at once are caught together.

X1114.2.p: A tall tale in which a tiger lies in water with its mouth open and a cat drives fish into its mouth.

X1115.p: A tall tale in which a hunter takes a huge bag of raccoons that are frozen together.

X1115.1.p: A tall tale in which rabbits are so cold that their feet freeze fast to the ice overnight, so the hunter gathers them up by the frozen feet.

X1116.p: A tall tale in which a hunter cuts down a tree so packed with animals that the tree's bark cracks open as the animals breathe in and close as they breathe out.

X1119.p: A collection of miscellaneous tall tales about hunting or fishing where game is absurdly plentiful.

X1119.1.p: A tall tale in which a hunter's bag includes a huge flock of birds, all brought down at once. The point of the story is the absurd exaggeration.

X1119.2.p: A tall tale in which a hunter boasts of an extraordinary number of deer taken in one hunt. The joke lies in the exaggerated count.

X1120.p: A tall tale about a hunter who is supposedly a superb marksman. The humor comes from his boasted, unbelievable skill with a gun.

X1121.p: A tall tale in which a supreme marksman owns a gun of extraordinary quality. The humor lies in the exaggerated gun.

X1122.p: A tall tale in which a hunter shows unbelievable skill with a gun. The boast is the basis of the joke.

X1122.1.p: A tall tale in which a hunter's shot carries an impossibly great distance. The joke is the exaggerated range of his bullet or arrow.

X1122.2.p: A tall tale in which one shot from a hunter kills many animals at once. The humor comes from the absurd number of kills.

X1122.3.p: A tall tale in which a clever person bends the barrel of a gun to make a spectacular shot. The trick is the absurd ingenuity.

X1124.p: A tall tale in which a hunter catches or kills game by an clever or unusual method that is far from ordinary. The humor lies in the unorthodox technique.

X1124.1.r: (First ed. X921.8.) An old blind bear is being led by a young bear, whose tail the old bear has in his mouth. The hunter shoots off the young bear’s tail and seizes it. Thus leads the old bear home. Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 748; U.S.: *Baughman.
X1124.1.p: A boastful lie in which a hunter shoots off the tail of a leading animal in a clever or unusual way.

X1124.2.r: (First ed. X911.1.) Wesselski Bebel II 137 No. 115; U.S.: *Baughman.
X1124.2.p: A tall tale in which a hunter turns an animal inside out. He reaches down its throat, grabs its tail, and pulls it inside out.

X1124.3.r: (First ed. X921.1.) Type 1890; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Friends 154 No. 21.
X1124.3.p: A tall tale in which a gun goes off by accident and kills a great deal of game. One bird falls onto a branch that drops on a bear, and so on in a chain of mishaps.

X1124.3.1.p: A tall tale in which an accidental gunshot splits a tree limb that then traps the feet of birds, catching them.

X1124.4.p: A tall tale in which a hunter catches wolves using a fishing rod and line. The humor lies in the absurd fishing method.

X1130.p: A tall tale about a hunter's strange and unlikely experiences. The humor comes from the bizarre events he claims to have had.

X1130.1.p: A tall tale in which game rolls downhill in the snow and a snowball grows around it. The snow keeps the game fresh and protected until it is used.

X1130.2.r: Compare Münchhausen (1944) 32 (cherry tree). Canada, U.S.: *Baughman; India: Thompson-Balys.
X1130.2.p: A tall tale in which a fruit tree grows from the head of a deer that was shot with fruit pits. The joke is the absurd growth.

X1130.2.1.p: A tall tale in which a tree grows out of a horse and gives its rider shade. It is an extension of the fruit tree growing from a shot deer.

X1130.3.p: A tall tale in which a lake or stream freezes just as frogs jump into it, so the frogs are trapped in the ice.

X1132.p: A tall tale about a hunter who skins an animal in a clever or unusual way. The humor lies in the ingenious skinning.

X1132.1.p: A tall tale in which a wolf's tail is nailed to a tree, and the wolf runs off and leaves its skin hanging behind.

X1133.p: A tall tale in which a hunter finds himself in serious danger, told as a boast of his unusual adventures.

X1133.1.p: A boastful tale in which a man climbs out of a tree stump by an astonishing method.

X1133.2.p: A tall tale in which a man flees a bear so long that the seasons change from summer to winter, until the bear finally falls through river ice or gives up.

X1133.3.r: (First ed. X911.) *Type 1875; Köhler-Bolte I 410; *Fb “tønde” III 935a, “ræv” III 114a.
X1133.3.p: A tall tale in which a man trapped in a barrel escapes by grabbing a passing wolf by the tail, which pulls him out.

X1133.3.1.p: An animal accidentally puts its tail into a man's hands and gets caught by it.

X1133.3.2.r: “What a dust.”—“If the wolf’s tail breaks, you will see another kind of dust!” (First ed. X911.3.) Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 216 No. 48; West Indies: Flowers 585.
X1133.3.2.p: A tale in which a wolf hunter's companion is blinded by dust when the wolf scratches while being caught by the tail; the outcome depends on whether the wolf's tail breaks.

X1133.4.p: A tall tale in which a man escapes from a bees' nest by riding out on a bear's tail.

X1133.5.p: A tall tale in which tigers stand on each other's heads in an attempt to reach a man hiding in a tree; his weeping forms a stream.

X1150.p: Tall tales about fishing, in which the catches and fishing methods are wildly exaggerated.

X1150.1.p: A tall tale about an enormous catch of fish.

X1151.p: A tall tale in which a huge crowd of fishermen gathers in one spot.

X1153.p: A tall tale in which fish are caught by an astonishing trick.

X1154.p: A tall tale about an unusual catch made by a fisherman.

X1154.1.p: A tall tale in which a fisherman catches a fish with astonishing things inside it.

X1154.1.1.p: A tall tale in which a man catches a fish that has a larger fish inside it.

X1156.p: Tall tales about other unusual ways of catching fish.

X1156.1.p: A tall tale in which fish are caught by calling out or shouting in another person's voice.

X1200.p: Tall tales about remarkable animals, exaggerating their size, abilities or traits.

X1201.p: A tall tale about an animal of enormous size or great power.

X1202.p: A tall tale in which animals pass on traits or conditions they acquired to their offspring.

X1202.1.p: A tall tale in which a crippled sow gets a small cart fitted as back legs to get around. The joke is that pigs are said to use such carts too.

X1203.r: (E.g. Pine tops: milk good for cough syrup.) U.S.: *Baughman.
X1203.p: A tall tale in which an animal's food has a strange, unlikely effect on it.

X1204.p: A tall tale in which animals devour one another, usually to an absurd extent.

X1204.1.p: A tall tale in which two wolves eat each other until only their tails are left.

X1204.2.p: A tall tale in which two birds swallow each other.

X1205.p: A tall tale in which the venom of an animal such as a snake, hornet or bee makes an object swell up enormously.

X1205.1.p: A tall tale in which a snake strikes an object and the object swells up as a result.

X1206.p: A tall tale in which animals are trained to respond to certain sounds, with an absurd result.

X1208.p: A tall tale in which animals come already cooked and ready to eat.

X1208.1.p: A tall tale in which roast pigs run around with a knife and fork stuck in their backs, ready to be eaten.

X1208.2.p: A tall tale in which roast hens fly up into the sky with their heads up and tails down.

X1210.p: A general heading for tall tales and lies about mammals.

X1211.p: A general heading for tall tales and lies about cats.

X1211.1.p: A tall tale in which a cat scratches out a bear's tongue.

X1211.2.p: A tall tale in which a crippled cat uses a wooden leg to kill mice.

X1212.p: A general heading for tall tales and lies about wildcats.

X1213.p: A general heading for tall tales and lies about panthers.

X1215.p: A general heading for tall tales and lies about dogs.

X1215.1.p: A tall tale in which a dog and another animal chase each other around in hot weather.

X1215.2.p: A tall tale about an impossibly large dog.

X1215.3.p: A tall tale about an impossibly small dog.

X1215.4.p: A tall tale in which a dog is so weak or feeble that it is presented as absurdly frail.

X1215.5.p: A tall tale in which a dog is described as absurdly tough, able to endure impossible hardship.

X1215.6.p: A tall tale in which a dog is described as absurdly fierce or savage.

X1215.7.p: A tall tale in which a dog is described as impossibly fast.

X1215.8.p: A tall tale in which a dog is described as impossibly clever.

X1756.1.p: A tall tale in which people are said to carry wine in baskets, ignoring that baskets leak. It is a joke built on an absurd disregard of what the container is like.

X1757.r: (First ed. X961.2.) (Cf. F843.) Type 852; BP II 513; Missouri French: Carrière.
X1757.p: A joke lie in which someone is said to have made or used a rope out of sand or chaff, which cannot be twisted into rope. It mocks the absurd ignoring of what a material is.

X1757.1.p: A variant of the sand-rope lie in which the rope is said to be made of dry dust, which likewise cannot be made into rope.

X1760.p: A category of tall tales that absurdly treat intangible things, such as sounds, shadows, or air, as if they were solid objects.

X1761.p: A category of tall tales that absurdly ignore the nature of holes, treating them as if they were solid things that can be handled or used.

X1761.1.p: A tall tale in which a man pulls up old oil wells, saws them into short lengths, and sells them as post holes. The joke treats a hole as if it were a solid object that can be cut up and sold.

X1761.2.p: A tall tale in which people are said to eat the bungholes from barrels, treating an opening as if it were something edible.

X1780.p: A category of tall tales whose absurdity comes from ignoring what a particular object is really like.

X1781.p: A category of tall tales about boats that can sail in impossibly shallow water, having an absurdly small draft.

X1781.1.p: A tall tale in which a boat sails over a dry river bed, the water being supposedly only rice water or similar thin liquid.

X1785.p: A category of tall tales about things that stretch or shrink in absurd ways.

X1785.1.p: A tall tale in which a man driving a wagon up a wet hill finds that the rawhide tugs have stretched so the load is still at the bottom. He leaves the harness on a stump, and the next day the sun shrinks the tugs and pulls the load up the hill.

X1787.p: A joke cure in which a man treats rheumatism with absurd ingredients, namely mosquito milk stirred in a cat's horn with a duck's crotch.

X1788.p: A tall tale about a painting so realistic that it is taken for the real thing or leads to absurd results.

X1790.p: A miscellaneous category of tall tales based on other kinds of logical absurdity.

X1791.p: A tall tale in which deaf, dumb, blind, and lame men are said to catch a hare, each contributing a disability that should prevent it.

X1796.p: A category of tall tales exaggerating speed in absurd ways.

X1796.1.p: A tall tale in which a man with no feet outruns a swift horse.

X1800.p: A general category of miscellaneous lies and exaggerations that do not fit elsewhere.

X1810.p: A category of tall tales about miscellaneous objects, exaggerated or impossible in their properties.

X1811.p: A general category of tall tales in which a teller lies about the enormous size or strange nature of bread loaves.

X1811.1.p: A tall tale in which the teller claims to have seen or made an enormous loaf of bread.

X1813.r: (First ed. X1036.) (Cf. B31.1.1.) *Fb “æg” III 1142a; U.S.: Baughman; India: Thompson-Balys.
X1813.p: A tall tale in which the teller claims to have seen or owned an enormous egg.

X1815.p: A tall tale in which the teller boasts of an extraordinary railroad.

X1815.1.p: A tall tale in which the teller claims a railroad was so rough that riding it was unusually bumpy.

X1815.2.p: A tall tale in which the teller jokes that trains travel so slowly that they are absurdly delayed.

X1817.p: A general category of tall tales in which the teller lies about bridges and their unusual features.

X1817.1.p: A tall tale in which a razor-sharp sword is used as a footbridge, so that crossing it is dangerous.

X1850.p: A miscellaneous group of tall tales that do not fit the more specific categories of lies and exaggeration.

X1851.p: A tall tale in which the man in the moon lowers himself down to earth.

X1852.p: A tall tale in which a boy is fired out of a cannon.

X1853.p: A tall tale in which a boy is described as wearing a hat made of butter and clothes made of paper.

X1854.p: A tall tale in which a man hiding in a hollow tree successfully fends off a leopard and a bear.

X1854.1.r: (First ed. X913.1.) Type 1877*; Russian: Andrejev No. 1877*.
X1854.1.p: A tall tale in which a boy hiding in a hollow tree frightens a woodchopper, who leaves his horse behind.

X1855.p: A tall tale in which a plow is described as working without a horse or wheels.

X1856.p: A tall tale in which nursing babies are said to rock their mother's cradle.

X1856.1.p: A tall tale in which a child is said to throw down a goat.

X1856.2.p: A tall tale in which a child is said to throw mill-wheels from one town to another.

X1857.p: A tall tale in which a man is said to have drowned on a mountain.

X1858.p: A tall tale in which a man is said to cut ice using his own head.

X1861.p: A tall tale about an absurdly long hunt for a bee that has been lost.

X1862.r: (First ed. X938.) Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 38 No. 288C*, Espinosa Jr. Nos. 59, 60; West Indies: Flowers 585.
X1862.p: A tall tale in which a hasty toad (or beetle) climbs a long flight of steps over many years, then falls on the last step and curses its haste.

X1863.r: (First ed. X953.) (Cf. X650.) Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. IX 85.
X1863.p: A joke explaining why Gypsies have no churches: they ate them, since their churches were made of cheese and bacon.

X1864.r: (First ed. X961.4.) Wesselski Bebel II 108 No. 25.
X1864.p: A tall tale in which a warrior's horse is cut in two, yet he keeps riding on the front half.

X1866.p: A tall tale about a bass viol that makes an enormous, far-reaching noise.
